overview.title: Training and evaluating the bigram model, and the limits of n-grams
overview.main_topic: Inspecting the bigram multi-hot encoding, training the unchanged linear classifier on it (30,001 parameters), reaching 90% test accuracy, and why n-grams beyond trigrams become intractable
overview.central_idea: With a shared unigram + bigram vocabulary of 30,000 terms, the same linear classifier improves from about 88% to 90% test accuracy at almost no extra cost. Going much beyond bigrams or trigrams fails: the space of word n-grams grows exponentially, so coverage needs immense vocabularies and the model starts memorizing snippets instead of generalizing.
overview.importance: It completes the set-model part of the chapter with its best result (90%) and gives the motivation for sequence models in section 14.5 (p.429).
learning_objectives: Interpret the batch shape (32, 30000) and the mixed unigram/bigram vocabulary slice
Explain why build_linear_classifier can be reused unchanged and why it now has 30,001 parameters
Explain why n-gram models beyond trigrams become intractable and overfit

summary:
The page continues from listing 14.16 (p.427). Pulling one batch from `bigram_train_ds` gives `x.shape == (32, 30000)`: each of 32 reviews is now a 30,000-dimensional multi-hot vector. Slicing the learned vocabulary, `text_vectorization.get_vocabulary()[100:108]` returns `["in a", "most", "him", "dont", "it was", "one of", "for the", "made"]`. Unigrams and bigrams sit side by side, ranked by frequency, which confirms that they compete for the same vocabulary slots. ("dont" also shows the default standardization stripping the apostrophe.)

Because only the encoding changed, the model needs no changes. **Listing 14.17** calls `build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, "bigram_classifier")` with `max_tokens = 30_000` and fits it for up to 10 epochs with the same `early_stopping` callback. The model has **30,001 parameters** instead of 20,001 but trains in about the same time.

**Listing 14.18** evaluates on `bigram_test_ds`: **0.90116**. That is 90% test accuracy, "a noticeable improvement" over the bag-of-words model's 0.88388 (p.426). The error rate drops from about 11.6% to 9.9%.

The last paragraph sets the limits. **Trigrams** (triplets of words) could help further, but beyond trigrams the problem quickly becomes **intractable**. The space of possible English 4-grams is immense and grows exponentially with n. Decent coverage would need an immense vocabulary, and the model would lose its ability to generalize, *memorizing entire snippets of sentences with weights attached*. Robustly modelling longer-range order needs more advanced techniques, which is the transition to the sequence models of section 14.5.

paragraphs.excerpt: If we look at a small subsection of our vocabulary, we can see both
paragraphs.what_it_says: A slice of the vocabulary shows both unigram and bigram terms.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Indices 100-107 hold very frequent terms: function-word bigrams ("in a", "it was", "one of", "for the") mixed with unigrams ("most", "him", "dont", "made"). Since the vocabulary is sorted by frequency, these bigrams are as common as mid-frequency words.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It confirms empirically the "compete for space" scheme described on p.427.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): "dont" comes from default standardization (lowercase + strip punctuation) applied to "don't", so the apostrophe is gone.

terminology.meaning: Returns the learned vocabulary list of a TextVectorization layer; index i corresponds to position i of the multi-hot vector.

connections: p.427: unigrams and bigrams compete for space in the same vocabulary

paragraphs.excerpt: With our new encoding for our input data, we can train a linear model
paragraphs.what_it_says: With the new encoding, the linear model can be trained unaltered from before.
paragraphs.what_it_means: All the bigram knowledge lives in the preprocessing. The model-building function from listing 14.13 just receives a different input size.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It shows the benefit of wrapping model construction in a function (p.424) and of keeping feature engineering separate from the model.
connections: p.424: build_linear_classifier was saved as a function to be reused later

paragraphs.excerpt: This model will be slightly larger than our bag-of words models (30,001 parameters
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model has 30,001 parameters instead of 20,001, but trains in about the same time.
paragraphs.what_it_means: One weight per vocabulary term (now 30,000) plus a bias. Training time barely changes because, as p.425 noted, tokenization and encoding are more expensive than the parameter updates. A 50% bigger dot product is still tiny.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The accuracy gain comes almost for free in compute.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Parameters of Dense(1) on an input of size d: $d \times 1 + 1$. For d = 30,000: 30,001.
connections: p.425: encoding the input costs more than updating the model parameters

paragraphs.excerpt: We’re now getting 90% test accuracy, a noticeable improvement!
paragraphs.what_it_says: Test accuracy is now 90%, a noticeable improvement.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Up from 88.4% (p.426) to 90.1%: about 1.7 points in absolute terms, or roughly 15% fewer errors (11.6% -> 9.9%).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It quantifies the value of local word order for sentiment.

paragraphs.excerpt: We could improve this number even further by considering trigrams (triplets of words)
paragraphs.what_it_says: Trigrams could improve accuracy further, but beyond trigrams the problem quickly becomes intractable. The space of possible English 4-grams is immense and grows exponentially as sequences get longer. Decent coverage of 4-grams would need an immense vocabulary, and the model would lose its ability to generalize, memorizing whole snippets of sentences with weights attached. Robustly using longer-range order needs more advanced modelling techniques.
paragraphs.what_it_means: With a word vocabulary of size V, there are up to $V^n$ possible n-grams. Each specific long n-gram is rare, so most appear only a few times in training. A weight learned for a rare 4-gram mostly memorizes the label of the few reviews that contained it, which is overfitting. Meanwhile most 4-grams in the test set were never seen and fall outside the vocabulary.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why set models plateau and motivates sequence models, which learn order-aware representations instead of listing phrases one by one.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: this is the sparsity / curse-of-dimensionality problem of n-gram models. Learned representations (embeddings, recurrent and attention layers) share statistical strength across similar contexts instead of treating every phrase as an unrelated feature.

terminology.meaning: A sequence of three consecutive tokens.
Growing so fast in size or cost that it cannot be handled in practice.

connections: p.429: 14.5 Sequence models introduces models that consider the full order of tokens

concepts.name: n-gram features and their limits
concepts.definition: Using sequences of n consecutive tokens as vocabulary terms in a set model.
concepts.intuition: Short phrases help, but long phrases are so varied that almost every one is new.
concepts.technical: Possible n-grams grow as $V^n$. Fixed-size vocabularies cover a shrinking fraction, and weights on rare n-grams memorize training snippets.
concepts.significance: Bigrams lift IMDb accuracy to 90%; 4-grams and beyond become intractable.
concepts.example: "in a", "it was", "one of" are frequent bigrams; a 4-gram like "one of the worst" is far rarer.
concepts.misconception: That larger n always helps. It eventually hurts generalization.

concepts.name: Overfitting via memorization
concepts.definition: Fitting training-specific details that don't generalize to new data.
concepts.intuition: Learning "this exact sentence fragment means positive" instead of a general pattern.
concepts.technical: Rare high-order n-gram features let a linear model assign a weight to the label of a few training reviews.
concepts.significance: The book's reason why n-gram models can't simply be extended to long sequences.
concepts.example: A 4-gram seen once in a positive review gets a positive weight that has nothing to do with sentiment.
concepts.misconception: That a linear model can't overfit. With enough sparse features it can memorize.

concepts.name: Reusing the model, changing the features
concepts.definition: Keeping build_linear_classifier fixed and changing only the input encoding.
concepts.intuition: A fair experiment that changes one variable at a time.
concepts.technical: Dense(1, sigmoid) on (None, 30000): 30,001 parameters; same optimizer, loss, epochs and early stopping.
concepts.significance: Attributes the 88% -> 90% gain to bigram features alone.
concepts.misconception: That the model had to be redesigned for bigrams.

math.title: Parameter count of the bigram classifier
math.operations: One weight per input feature plus one bias for a single-unit Dense layer.
math.purpose: Explains the parameter numbers quoted in the text.
math.interpretation: Each vocabulary term (unigram or bigram) has exactly one weight.

math.title: Growth of the n-gram space
math.source_text: the problem grows exponentially as sequences get longer and longer
math.operations: Each of the n positions can hold any of V words.
math.interpretation: Only a small fraction of these occur in real text, but the number that do still grows very quickly with n, so a fixed vocabulary covers less and less.
math.intuition: Each extra word in the phrase multiplies the possibilities.
math.numerical_example: With V = 20,000: bigrams up to $4\times10^8$, trigrams up to $8\times10^{12}$, 4-grams up to $1.6\times10^{17}$.

deeper.title: How big is the improvement, really?
deeper.body: Errors: unigram $1 - 0.88388 = 0.11612$, bigram $1 - 0.90116 = 0.09884$. Relative error reduction: $(0.11612 - 0.09884)/0.11612 \approx 14.9\%$. On the 25,000-review IMDb test set, that is roughly $0.01728 \times 25{,}000 \approx 430$ more reviews classified correctly. (The test set size is from the dataset loaded on p.420; this calculation is not in the book.)

deeper.title: Why longer n-grams memorize instead of generalize
deeper.body:
1. Longer n-grams are rarer: most specific 4-grams appear in only one or two training reviews.
2. A linear model gives each n-gram feature its own weight, and nothing ties the weight of "one of the worst" to that of "among the very worst".
3. A feature seen once can be given a weight that simply reproduces that review's label: memorization.
4. At test time most 4-grams were never seen and are out of vocabulary, so these weights rarely apply.

This is why the book says more advanced techniques are needed for longer-range order.

deeper.title: Phrasebook vs. grammar
deeper.body: An n-gram model is like a tourist phrasebook: great for common two-word phrases, but you can't print every possible sentence. Sequence models are more like learning the grammar, so you can understand combinations you've never seen.

takeaways: The bigram encoding produces batches of shape (32, 30000), with unigrams and bigrams interleaved in a frequency-ranked vocabulary.
The linear classifier is reused unchanged and has 30,001 parameters; training time is about the same.
Trigrams might help a bit more, but beyond that the n-gram space explodes and models memorize instead of generalizing.
Longer-range word order needs sequence models (section 14.5).

questions.question: Why does x.shape equal (32, 30000) for a batch of bigram_train_ds?
questions.answer: 32 is the batch size, and 30,000 is max_tokens: the multi-hot vector has one position per vocabulary term (unigram or bigram).

questions.question: Which entry in the vocabulary slice is a unigram?
questions.explanation: "dont" is one token ("don't" with the apostrophe stripped); the other three are two-word bigrams.

questions.question: How many parameters does build_linear_classifier produce for max_tokens = 30,000, and how many more than the bag-of-words model?
questions.answer: 30,001 parameters; 10,000 more than the 20,001 of the unigram model.
questions.explanation: Dense(1) has one weight per input plus one bias: 30,000 + 1.

questions.question: What test accuracy does the bigram model reach?
questions.explanation: Listing 14.18 prints 0.90116. 0.88388 is the unigram model (p.426); the others are not on the page.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the book offers for why n-gram models beyond trigrams become impractical.
questions.answer: (1) The space of possible 4-grams is immense and grows exponentially with length, so decent coverage needs an immense vocabulary. (2) The model would lose its ability to generalize, memorizing entire snippets of sentences with weights attached.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the last paragraph; together they motivate the more advanced sequence models.

questions.question: Why does the bigram model train in about the same time despite having 50% more parameters?
questions.answer: The model is tiny either way; training cost is dominated by tokenizing and encoding text on the CPU rather than by the parameter updates.
questions.explanation: p.425 noted that encoding is more expensive than updating the parameters, and the page says it trains in about the same amount of time.

questions.question: Can you explain why reusing build_linear_classifier unchanged makes the 88% -> 90% comparison meaningful?
questions.answer: Only the features changed (unigrams -> unigrams + bigrams); architecture, optimizer, loss, epochs and early stopping stayed the same, so the gain can be attributed to the bigram features.
questions.explanation: This is a controlled experiment that changes one variable at a time.
